title: Are Jump Shots Legal in Pool? A Beginner's Guide to the Rules
description: Can you jump the cue ball in pool? A plain-English look at what the WPA rules say about jump shots, scoops and jump cues, and when they are a foul.
body:
Picture this: the cue ball is hiding right behind your opponent's ball, and the shot you need is on the other side. Someone at the table whispers, "Just jump it!" But is that even allowed? The honest answer is the one pool players love to give: it depends on the game you are playing and the rules in the room.

What is a jump shot?

A jump shot is any shot where the cue ball is made to travel over something in its way, such as another ball or part of the cushion. The World Pool-Billiard Association (WPA) rulebook describes it the same way, and adds that whether the shot is legal depends on how it is done and what the shooter intended.

The key phrase in the WPA rules is how a legal jump is played: the player raises the cue stick and drives the cue ball down into the playing surface, so the ball rebounds up off the cloth. In other words, you aim downward and let the table push the ball into the air.

The scoop: why it is a different story

There is a sneaky way to make the cue ball rise that the rules treat differently. If the tip touches the cloth and the cue ball at the same moment and the ball lifts off the table, the WPA rules treat that like a miscue. An accidental miscue that makes the ball hop is treated as a legal jump shot. But a miscue done on purpose falls under the rule on unsportsmanlike conduct.

The takeaway for beginners: learn the downward-strike jump, not the scoop. It is the cleaner, more honest technique, and it is the one the rules describe.

Where jumping is allowed, and where it is a foul

In the WPA rules for the big international games, such as 9-ball and 10-ball, the general jump-shot definition applies, and the rules even allow players to switch between a break cue, a jump cue and a normal cue during a match. That is why you will see pros reach for a special jump cue in tournaments.

But not every game works that way. In the WPA's Blackball (a British-style pool game) rules, causing the cue ball to jump over any ball is listed as a standard foul. So a shot that is perfectly fine in one game can cost you the table in another.

  • Pro-style 9-ball and 10-ball: a legal downward jump is part of the game, and jump cues are allowed.
  • Blackball: jumping the cue ball over a ball is a foul.
  • Bar and league play: local rules may be stricter. Many places ban jump shots, jump cues or both, so ask before you try one.

For a refresher on how fouls work and what ball in hand means, see our guide to common pool fouls. And our page on bar rules versus tournament rules explains why the same shot can be legal at one table and illegal at the next.

Always ask first at a bar table

Here is some friendly advice that comes from common sense rather than any rulebook: a jump shot can mark or damage the cloth if it goes wrong, and bar owners know it. Before you try one on a public table, check the house rules and ask the owner or your opponent. It is polite, and it keeps everyone friends.

How beginners can start practicing

Treat these as general coaching ideas rather than official rules, and take it slowly:

  1. Get permission and pick the right place. Practice on a table where jumping is allowed, ideally one you own or one the room says is fine.
  2. Start with a big gap. Place a ball a few inches in front of the cue ball and try to clear it. Cue ball and object ball that are almost touching are much harder.
  3. Raise the back of the cue. The steeper your cue, the more the ball pops up. Keep your grip and bridge steady.
  4. Strike down, then follow through. Aim to hit the cue ball and drive it into the cloth, rather than scooping underneath.
  5. Practice control, not just height. Jumping over a ball is only half the job; the ball also has to land where you want. Our aiming guide helps with the second half.

Do you even need to jump?

Often, no! Before you reach for a jump cue, look for a kick shot off one rail, which is perfectly legal and works in almost every game. We cover it in our guide on how to kick in pool. Knowing both options makes you a smarter, calmer player when a ball blocks your path.

Where to see jump shots live

The best way to understand when pros choose to jump is to watch them. Browse the tournament listings to find events near you, or check the event calendar for upcoming big events. Watching a few matches will show you how rarely, and how carefully, top players decide to jump.

The bottom line

Jump shots are real, legal and exciting in many pool games, as long as they are played by driving the cue ball down into the table. They are a foul in others, like Blackball, and many bars say no. When in doubt, check the rules and ask first.

What do you think: do jump shots belong in pool, or should the cue ball stay on the cloth?
